speechtext: That the report of the special committee appointed to prepare and report with all convenient speed the lists of members to compose the select standing committees of this House during the present session, presented this day, be concurred in.
Motion agreed to.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING moved:
speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: That the select standing committees of this House shall severally be empowered to examine and inquire into all such matters and things as may be referred to them by the House, and to report from time to time their observations and opinions thereon, with power to send for persons, papers and records, with the exception of the committee on Debates and that on the Library of Parliament.
Motion agreed to.

speechtext: At the conclusion of last session the hon. member for Comox-Alberni (Mr. Neill) spoke to me about the negotiations that were proceeding between the government of Canada and the government of Japan in respect to the restriction of immigration from Japan, and asked if I would inform the House at that time whac progress had been made with these negotiations. I intimated that I was not in a position to bring down the correspondence at the time, but that I would do so as soon as the House reassembled. I desire now to lay on the Table copies of the correspondence between the governments of Japan and Canada with respect to the subject of restriction of immigration. My hon. friend will see that the Japanese government do not, under the administrative measures now adopted, contemplate that the number of Japanese emigrants going to Canada as household servants and agricultural labourers will exceed 160 annually.

speakername: Hon. Mr. ROBB (For the Minister of Railways and Canals):

speechtext: Is it a fact that through some carelessness in the Finance Department during the war, that Canada will lose twenty-four million dollars in exchanges?

The hon. Imember's
question is answered in the negative.
In the settlement of financial matters between the Imperial and Canadian Governments, the question arose as to the rate at which sterling advances to Canada in London would be credited against the Imperial Government s indebtedness to Canada in dollars. Canada advanced a claim based upon the current rate of exchange. The Imperial Treasury officials resisted this. They con-.ended that certain ''sot-oil's''' under which by agreement the book debts had been reduced at intervals by wiping off certain amounts of sterling advances against an equivalent amount of dollar advances, were to be regarded as finally settled at the par rate of exchange. They further pointed out that it would have been quite beyond the contemplation of the Treasury to have incurred such a heavy exchange charge, and that the alternative would be to consider the total Canadian advances as a debt to be settled by Britain in dollars when that could be done

or when exchange reached par. Negotiations having resulted in failure to reach an agreement satisfactory to both sides, a friendly arbitration was arranged for by the present Minister of Finance (Mr. Fielding) with Rt. Hon. Mr. Asquith as arbitrator, the result of which, namely the award to Canada of $8,199,333 by way of exchange, was announced to the House last session.

I mentioned a day or two ago that when the estimates were brought down hon. members would be able to see the intention of the government with respect to the bonus to be given to civil servants. The relevant item will be found on page 61, of the estimates just tabled, under "Miscellaneous", it is item 363, and reads-
Provisional bonus allowance for the inside and outside services of the Civil Service, to be paid to such persons and classes of persons, in such amounts and at such times as the Governor in Council may determine : $3,800,000.
That is $1,700,000 less than the amount which this House voted at the last session for bonus to be paid civil servants in addition to their salaries. The government did not feel, in view of the retrenchment which they are finding it necessary to make and seeking to make, that they would be justified in longer continuing the bonus to members of the Civil Service who are unmarried, and who have no one dependent on them. On the other hand, with respect to members of the service who are married, or unmarried members of the service who have one or more persons dependent on them, it was represented to the government very strongly from many quarters, that to withdraw the bonus in their case pending a revision of civil service salaries might work a considerable hardship. This aspect of the matter was brought to the attention of the government more particularly by the hon. members for Ottawa who, perhaps, more than any other members of the House, are familiar with the circumstances of many members of the Civil Service, and the government have taken carefully into consideration such representations as they and others have made.
With respect to members of the Civil Service other than those who are unmarried and have no one dependent on them, the government proposes, as respects all such as are receiving a salary of $1,200 and tfnder, to continue the bonus at the rate at which it was continued last year. With respect to members in the service receiving a salary of over $1,200 and up to $1,560 inclusive, the government proposes to continue the bonus at the rate of two-thirds of the amount which is being paid at the present time. To those receiving over $1,560 and up to $1,800 inclusive, one-third of the present bonus will be continued. In other cases the bonus will be discontinued.
I should mention as related to this matter of the bonus that the government intends to have an immediate revision made of the sal-

Civil Service Bonus
aries of the Civil Service. It is our intention to ask the Civil Service Commission to undertake this work in conjunction with the deputy heads of the government departments and the Audit Board which has been appointed under legislation enacted last session, they will be asked to report to the government what, in their opinion, should be done by way of revision of the salaries of the civil servants. When the report is received, the government will take such action on its recommendations as in the circumstances appear to be warranted and justifiable. I should say also, in connection with this revision of salaries, that the government will seek to have provision made whereby the members of the Civil Service themselves, through their representatives, may appear before the commission and be taken into conference in the matter.
There is a feature that perhaps it is well to mention namely that at the time the bonus was added to the salaries of the Civil Service, there was a great deal of unemployment throughout the country. It was very difficult for persons to obtain ready admission into other employment, should they leave the service. Conditions in that particular have considerably improved. There is the further fact that from the time the bonus was first given, there have been in the case of most of those who are permanent in the service, statutory increases, year by year, which have increased considerably the amounts they were receiving at the time the bonus was first granted. The government realises that this is a very difficult question to deal with, and in announcing what I am at the moment, I am putting before the House what after very careful consideration of the interests of the civil servants and the public interest has seemed to the government the wise course to adopt.
I should mention also that the government intends at the present session to introduce a Superannuation Act. It has been felt that to complete the work of reorganisation of the Civil Service, as this reorganisation has already been undertaken and is being carried on in part by the Audit Board, it was desirable, in order that justice may be done those who are in the service at present and whose services may be dispensed with or who may subsequently enter the service, that a Superannuation Act should be immediately put through. The bill will be introduced in this House at the present session.

speakeroldname: Mr. T. L. CHURCH (North Toronto) moved:

speechtext:
That, in the opinion of this House, subject to certain reasonable charges including a certain sum for overhead expenses, lapsed policies of life insurance of companies with federal charters should be returned to the insured, and that in the interests of the insured such confiscatory powers of these companies should be further revised.
He said: The purpose of this resolution is to guarantee to the public the full benefit under all insurance policy contracts. This matter has been referred to by the Department of Insurance of the government in their reports for some years past. My motion would provide that, in the case of lapsed policies there should be a certain return to the insured. It means, not that the whole sum should be returned, but that the sum, subject to reasonable charges, as the resolution says, should be returned to these unfortunates. This motion is to press the government to have parliament look into the recommendations of their own insurance



Life Insurance-Lapsed Policies
advisers and to see if they cannot amenl the statute accordingly. Last session was devoted very largely to the Bank Act for the protection of depositors, and as regards life insurance, it is not altogether fair to the poorer class that their policies should lapse. These insurance companies take in millions of dollars in lapsed policies, and we seek protection against such confiscatory powers as life insurance companies have at present. The present law is not altogether fair to the man of small means; he is fighting a large corporation. The war has made a great difference in this respect. If you look over the report of the Department of Insurance, you will find that in a table on page 7 the amount is going up from year to year-especially during and since the war-of lapsed policies of people who are not able to pay their insurance premiums and whose policies are taken away from them by law. The amount runs into millions of dollars. Many of these people in days like these are out of work through no fault of their own; many of them are returned men who have been driven to the wall by hard times and the high cost of living, and the first thing to go has been the insurance policy, because the premiums cannot be kept up. As regards the high cost of living to-day, the table speaks for itself; it shows that in comparison with other countries, Canada is at the top of the list. The money held by these companies really consists of funds that rightfully belong to the estates of these unfortunate people, who permitted their policies to lapse after making a sufficient number of annual premium payments to give their policies some insurance value. I would suggest that the law be amended so as to provide that, after a sufficient deduction is made for overhead expenses, the policy holders should have a substantial part of their premiums paid them. The money confiscated by these companies consists of funds which rightly belong to the estates of unfortunate persons who in hard times were driven to allow their policies to lapse, after having made a sufficient number of annual premium payments to give those policies a paid-up or substantial insurance value. Some of the companies are lax in not acquainting the poorer policy holders with the law in regard to lapsed policies. The law provides that after a period of three years a policy holder shall have a claim upon the company in the event of a policy lapsing; but some of the companies are not informing the policy holders of this fact. The Insurance Act, like the Bank Act, needs revision. In the United States the statistics show that in the past twenty-five 
years policies have lapsed to the extent of $10,000,000,000, and a survey of conditions in Canada should, I think, be made to discover the losses to the working classes in this country from this source. If such a survey were made I believe that a similar state of things would be revealed. The failure of companies fully to advise their policy holders of the value of their policies is responsible in part for this condition. Many persons-who have permitted their policies to lapse do not know that such policies have a value if they have been in force for more than three years, and it has been pointed out that the insurance companies, taking advantage of this ignorance on the part of the public, have failed to notify the holders of lapsed policies of such value. I do not say that the companies all do this deliberately; but undoubtedly, through negligence at any rate, the policy holders are made to suffer in this way.
It is only fair, however, as pointed out by the Superintendent of Insurance, to say on behalf of the companies that, as in everything else, there are two sides to this argument. Section 180 of the Insurance Act of 1917 provides for a surrender value on policies of which three or more annual premiums have been paid. Sub-section 4 of this section provides for extended insurance until the cash surrender value is accepted or until the surrender value has been used up. And in the case of a policy lapsing when in force only a short time, both the insured and the company suffer. The policy holder loses the status he has achieved from beginning his insurance policy and acquiring the protection, and the company loses the business before it becomes profitable, as the cost to the company of acquiring new business is often in excess of the first premium. These are the views of the Superintendent of Insurance as expressed in a letter written to myself. He concludes:
As to the amount of the cash surrender value, it should always be borne in mind that while the policy is being in force the company is liable for the face of the policy which liability is worth something to the insured and the cost of which must be deducted in arriving at the cash surrender value.
In Ontario there has been a great deal of complaint in this direction in regard to provincial companies. Many friendly societies have not been able to make ends meet and have by legislation cut down the amount of the policy and raised their rates, and I would suggest that when an investigation is made into this matter it should

vincial companies and those doing business under a federal and provincial charter. In the larger cities the condition is serious, and from the district which I represent I have received many letters from insured persons complaining of the remissness of the companies along the lines I have indicated. The loss ratios by provinces for the year 1923 as compared with the year 1922 show on the whole an increase. In this connection I might read the following statement from the Inspector of Insurance made on the first day of October, 1923:
The total amount of business lapsed and surrendered in 1922 in Canada amounted to $288,838,320. Five years ago, in 1917, the total new business effected in Canada was $282,120,430. The business lapsed and surrendered in 1922 amounted to 50 per cent of the gross business issued. So long as this high rate of premature discontinuance prevails life insurance will fail to convey the benefits which by its very nature it is designed to convey to the insuring public, and it is to be hoped that investigation will lead to the discovery of the cause of this form of waste and to its ultimate removal.
Many of the companies are being criticized in Canada, and the other day one company was ordered by the department to deposit $50,000 more and additional security for the protection of its policyholders in order to hold up the financial end of the concern. I think there should be a survey made of all the companies before they fail. Who would have suspected before last June that the Home Bank would collapse? According to some of the pamphlets that were put out by the Bankers' Association, people thought it was almost impossible for shareholders or depositors to lose their money. It all goes to show that the whole insurance situation needs a revision in the interests of the insured. The same catastrophe that overtook the Home Bank might to-morrow occur in connection with the insurance companies. There is necessity of a thorough survey of all insurance companies, from the financial and other standpoints for the protection of policy holders. There can be no doubt of its necessity. In the last annual report of the Canada Life, one of the best companies we have in Canada, the following statement appears:
It is unfortunately unavoidable that some policy holders should through various circumstances find it impossible to continue their insurance, and during the past two or three years these terminations the world over have been aggravated by prevailing conditions. We have not escaped our share of this misfortune but, despite it, we have made the very substantial gain of 451,454,000 in our total assurances, bringing them up to $412,435,000. We have again been favoured with unusually low death losses, reflecting not only a generally good public health but a careful valuation by our selection committee of the lives offered us.

Before I conclude, Mr. Speaker, let me express the hope that the government will see to it that the recommendations of the Superintendent of Insurance be carried out and that in the recess of parliament some independent inquiry and survey be made of the whole insurance situation with regard to the solvency of the companies and from the point of view of their compliance with the law and their whole affairs. If the minister can give me some assurance that this will be done I shall be glad to withdraw the resolution. T suggest, however, that he should endeavour to carry out the very able and very sensible recommendations which have emanated from his own department. The department is a very good one and the report to which I have referred is a very fine report. I hope that the minister will encourage the officials to extend this inquiry and to see to it that the law is enforced and that the smaller policy holders and those whose policies have lapsed get additional protection.

Mr. Speaker, the mover of this resolution (Mr. Church) has touched upon a very important feature of our business and of our national life. His remarks, I may say, went much further than the resolution goes, and I am inclined to agree with his remarks rather than with the resolution itself.
It is very important that the insurance business should be thoroughly investigated by a committee of this House, just as the banking business should be investigated. The resolution refers to on: aspect of the matter, but there are also other features which should be considered. The amount of life insurance done in this country is tremendous and the number of policies in force is very large. I believe that the insurance companies have had a comparatively easy time in getting money for which in many cases they do not give a proper return. One question has been brought to my attention which should, it seems to me receive consideration, and that is in regard to participating policies, as they call them. I am told that in the United States no insurance company is allowed to write both participating and non-participating policies; that is, a company must choose which form of policy it will issue or which form of business it will do. In Canada, however, our insurance companies may write either participating or non-participating policies, and I am told that in the case of non-participating policies the policy holders are in many instances paying money for which they get no return of any consequence; that is to

say, they pay an exrra premium for the privilege of participating in the profits of the company but they have no chance in the world of even getting back the amount that they are paying by way of extra premium. If that is so, these insurance companies are taking the people's money for nothing. That of course does not apply to all insurance companies. I think this is a matter which should be thoroughly investigated. I am strongly of the opinion that the subject of insurance is one which should receive the attention of the House, and I suggest that the proper way of doing it would be to refer the whole question of life insurance business in Canada to a proper committee of the House.

Mr. JOS. T. SHAW (West Calgary) moved:
That, in the opinion of this House, legislation should be introduced in order to place the wife on an equality with the husband as regards the grounds upon which divorce may be obtained.

He said: Mr. Speaker, the resolution which I present to the Houso js very narrow in its compass and will not, I think, be the subject of much debate. At the outset I would like to make it abundantly clear that the resolution does not propose in any way to widen the grounds for divorce. I quite realize that many members of the House, and certainly a large number of persons outside the Iloust, have conscientious objections to the granting of divorces, but this resolution aims only to place the husband and the wife upon exactly the same plane so far as the grounds for divorce are concerned.
The law of divorce in Canada has been described as a patchwork law, and I think it has probably been correctly described. I want just for a moment to indicate the situation as I understand it to-day. The federal government has exclusive jurisdiction in matters of marriage and divorce, but it was provided in the British North America Act, by which this exclusive jurisdiction was vested in the federal government, that the laws in force in the various confederating provinces and the courts in existence therein were to be continued until repealed nr altered by some competent authority. Then by another section of the British North America Act it was provided that a similar provision should apply to provinces that might subsequently join the 'confederation. Now under those circumstances it is necessary for one to ascertain the conditions in the various provinces. ' Nova Scotia, New Brunswick and Prince Edward Island before confederation each had a divorce court operating in those provinces, and those courts are in existence to-day. In Nova Scotia either party to a marriage contract may secure a divorce on the grounds of adultery, impotence, cruelty or consanguinity. In New Brunswick divorce may be secured on the grounds of adultery, impotence or consanguinity; in Prince Edward Island the grounds are impotence, adultery or consanguinity. These courts, as I say, are constituted and organized and are effective today so far as granting divorces is concerned. In those Maritime provinces there is no question whatever but that the wife and the husband stand on exactly the same ground so far as the causes for divorce are concerned. Now, in the provinces of Ontario and Quebec, -and with respect to the latter province I speak subject to correction by my legal friends from Quebec,-there are no divorce courts, that is, no courts which have jurisdiction in granting divorces or dissolutions of the marriage tie.

Divorce
Turning our eyes westward for a few moments I would like to direct the attention of the House to the situation in the four western provinces. Manitoba, Saskatchewan and Alberta each have divorce courts. These courts in divorce matters are governed by the English law as it stood on the 15th of July, 1870. The courts of the province of British Columbia having jurisdiction in divorce matters are governed by the English law as it stood on the 19th of November, 1858. The result of this is that in the four western provinces the Matrimonial Causes Act passed by the Imperial parliament in 1857 is in full operation and effect.

speechtext: That has been amended recently, has it not?

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS
subsubtopic: EQUALITY OF GROUNDS FOR RELIEF AS BETWEEN THE SEXES
speechtext:
The law of England has been amended, and I shall come to that in a moment. The section of that act to which I wish to draw the attention of the House reads as follows:
It shall be lawful for any 'husband to present a petition to the said court, praying that his marriage may be dissolved, on the ground that his wife has 6ince the celebration thereof been guilty of adultery; and it shall be lawful for any wife to present a petition to the said court praying that her marriage may be dissolved, on the ground that since the celebration thereof her husband has been guilty of incestuous adultery, or bigamy with adultery, or of rape, or of sodomy, such cruelty as without adultery would have entitled her to a divorce a mensa et thoro, or of adultery coupled with desertion, without reasonable excuse for two years or upwards; and every such petition shall state as distinctly as the nature of the case permits the facts on which the claim to have such marriage dissolved is founded: Provided that for the purpose of this act incestuous adultery shall be taken to mean adultery committed by a husband with a woman with whom if his wife were dead he could not lawfully contract marriage by reason of her being within the prohibited degrees of consanguinity or affinity; and bigamy shall be taken to mean marriage of any person, being married to any other person during the life of the former husband or wife, whether the second marriage shall have taken place within the Dominion of Her Majesty or elsewhere.
Translated into ordinary simple English this section means that while a husband may secure a divorce from his wife on the ground of adultery, the wife must, in order to succeed, be able to substantiate one of the following charges:	1. Incestuous adultery; 2. Bigamy
with adultery; 3. Rape; 4. Sodomy or bestiality. And next we come to the two grounds to which I wish to particularly direct the attention of the House; they are adultery coupled with such cruelty as without adultery would justify judicial separation, and adultery coupled with desertion without reasonable excuse for two years or upward.
That is the English law as it stood in 1870, and those are the grounds only on which a married woman could secure a divorce from her husband. Why was equality denied in England, you may very well ask, at this particular time? Well, the debates of that day indicate that one of the main reasons was that men made the law, and the second reason given was that adultery was considered a more grievous offence against the wife than against the husband because of the possibility of the introduction of illegitimate children into the family. In other words, by this particular legislation the law created a monopoly so far as redress was concerned in the interests of the husband. It is rather interesting, however, to note that even in that day there were staunch advocates of equality between the husband and the wife. Lord Lyndhurst, in a very able address in the British House of Lords, presented the view for equality, and may I be permitted just for a few moments to read to the House the statements of Mr. Gladstone in that debate. Mr. Gladstone himself was conscientiously opposed to the granting of divorces, but he urged equality as between the sexes in these words:
For my own part I shall always assert the principle of equal rights. It is impossible to do a greater mischief than to begin now, in the middle of the 19th century, to undo, with regard to womankind, that which has already been done in their behalf, by slow degrees, in the preceding 18 centuries, and to say that the husband shall be authorized to dismiss his wife on grounds for which the wife shall not dismiss the husband. If there is one broad and palpable result of Christianity, which we ought to regard as precious, it is that it has placed the seal of God Almighty upon the equality of man and woman with respect to everything that relates to these rights: and I will offer the utmost resistance to any attempt to induce this House to adopt a measure which, I believe, would lead to the degradation of woman.
Now how does the legislation work out in actual practice in the four western provinces? As I have already pointed out in order to secure a divorce the woman is called upon to prove something more than the man is called upon to prove. She must in addition to adultery prove legal cruelty or she must prove desertion. Now one naturally questions the meaning of cruelty. If one were to examine the dictionary one would ascertain that it means inhuman treatment, or a disposition to inflict unnecessary pain or suffering on others, but in its legal sense the word has an altogether different meaning. I want to read from a judgment of the Appellate Court of Ontario which gives in a very few words the exact legal definition of cruelty.
To establish cruelty one must show treatment likely to produce or which produces physical illness or mental distress of a nature calculated permanently to affect her bodily health or endanger her reason, and that there
Divorce

is reasonable apprehension that the same state of things will continue.
These words are taken from a decision of the Appellate Court, in 1920. It is rather interesting to note, however, that Chief Justice Meredith, while he reluctantly agreed with the decision added these significant words:
The law is not in accord with modern views as to the relations between husband and wife. That it is such is to be deplored. Her life may be made a veritable hell upon earth and she is without remedy if robust enough to suffer it all without impairment of her physical health or her mentality.

speechtext: Is it not a fact that in several of the provinces where there are divorce courts the majority of judges, although cruelty is given as a ground for divorce as well as adultery, interpret cruelty to mean adultery?

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS
subsubtopic: EQUALITY OF GROUNDS FOR RELIEF AS BETWEEN THE SEXES
speechtext:
No, cruelty is never interpreted to mean adultery. I presume my hon. friend means that perhaps the courts, upon finding adultery presume cruelty. I take it that, perhaps, is what he means by his question. If my hon. friend will listen to these few instances I propose to quote he will see that his view is not the interpretation which the law bears in the various cases I wish to mention. In an Alberta case cited as B. vs. B. and found at page 894 of Volume 3 of the Weekly Western Reports for the year 1919, Mr. Justice Scott, now Chief Justice Scott, held that-"the fact that on one occasion a husband came home drunk and called his wife vile names before other people did not constitute legal cruelty sufficient together with acts of adultery to entitle her to divorce, the admitted adultery alone not entitling her to divorce."
In the 1921 case of Torsell vs. Torsell, reported at page 200 in 16 A.L.R. Chief Justice Harvey in giving the judgment of the appellate court used this language:
It has been accepted in England that legal cruelty to support a wife's claim must be such as to cause danger to life, limb or health present or future. There may be much room for dissatisfaction, but that is a matter which can be easily and effectively cured by the legislature if it desires.
In that case untrue charges of infidelity were made publicly by a husband. In Saskatchewan I find the case of Moon vs. Moon in the year 1913, reported in 6 S.L.R. at page 41. In that case the husband accused his wife, in the presence of a thirteen-year-old daughter, of adultery and under circumstances greatly aggravating the offence. The judge held these facts did not constitute legal cruelty, but he significantly added that he was pleased to have the English authority 
of Russel vs. Russell with which to justify his ruling. All these cases, I may say, are based upon a judgment in the year 1790 in the Matrimonial and Ecclesiastical court in England, and the latest accepted exposition of the law is the case of Russell vs. Russell, decided in England in 1895 by a 5 to 4 decision of the House of Lords. British Columbia courts afford some instances of similar rulings. In Walsh vs. Walsh, reported at page 482 in 20 B.C.R. in the year 1914, it appears that the wife stated that she became nervous because her husband kept a razor and sharp knife under his pillow in the bed where both slept. The husband stated that he wished to protect himself. The wife asked -I am quoting from the record-" Why do you want to protect yourself? " To which the husband answered, " I thought you might do me some harm while I was sleeping." The court held that legal cruelty was not established, that mere nervousness was not sufficient, and that the wife had not stated that she feared acts of violence, or that the weapons were kept by him for that purpose.
Let me also quote the Manitoba case of Dorset v. Dorset, decided in 1921 and reported in 57 D.L.R. at page 636. In that case the husband's adultery in his own residence was clearly proven. The court held that the husband's adultery in his own residence, where his wife stayed during a period of convalescence, did not constitute legal cruelty entitling her to divorce because the evidence did not show that her health was thereby impaired. In that case Chief Justice Mathers used this language:
Respondent's conduct in brazenly committing adultery with a paramour without any attempted concealment and in utter disregard of all decency no doubt constituted cruelty in the popular sense but not in a legal sense.
I am not stating these cases for the purpose of criticizing the courts, because I think the courts have followed precedents and have given, in my humble judgment, correct interpretations of the law. I do so, for the purpose of showing the difficulties that a wife labours under in the four western provinces when she seeks to establish her right to divorce, even where adultery on the part of her husband is admitted. Nor is that all. The courts require that the cruelty should be corroborated, and if anyone questions that I would refer them to the English ease of Judd vs. Judd, which was decided in the year 1907 by the probate division in England. Now, it is seldom that the husband commits either adultery or cruelty in public, and if when adultery is committed the wife must have cor-

Divorce
roborative evidence to prove the cruelty then you can understand the difficulty and the tremendous handicap under which she, in my judgment, wrongly labours. On the other hand suppose the wife, in addition to proving the adultery, does not rely upon legal cruelty but is forced to rely on the ground of desertion for two years and upwards. Hon members will note that the statute reads:
Desertion for upwards of two years without reasonable excuse.
Now, the words "without reasonable excuse" afford a very wide latitude for a husband to escape from the consequences of his conduct. The situation then, Mr. Speaker, is clearly this-that a husband may indulge in every variety of infamy connected with adultery, he may use every refinement of cruelty short of legal cruelty, and he may violate every human law, and yet escape the proper and legitimate consequences of his act. That is the situation, in short, in the four western provinces. Of course it may be urged that parliament grants divorces. That is quite true. The parliament of Canada does grant divorce, and applicants before this parliament stand on an even footing. But I need only point out, that if one examines the list of applications for divorce from the western provinces you will find comparatively* few. The initial expense-the fees totalling something like $210-is of itself a considerable deterrent. To that must be added the expense of attendance in the city of Ottawa; the expense of the attendance of witnesses in this city perhaps for longer or shorter periods; and the result is that so far as the parliament of Canada is concerned it is practically inaccessible to women who contemplate applications for divorce.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS

speechtext:
Quite right. I mentioned that in opening. The British North America Act protects the rights of the Maritime provinces and other provinces in that regard. The Matrimonial Causes Act of 1857, by which our four western provinces are governed now, is not now the law of England. In the year 1912 a very representative commission was appointed in England for the purpose of going into this whole subject of divorce, and it made a report to parliament. It is a very comprehensive report. The individuals who composed that commission are security enough to show that the whole matter was thoroughly and amply ventilated. They called witnesses from every part of England, and from practically every walk in life, and representatives of every religious denomination. As a result of their report, while they disagreed upon some things, they at least were unanimous on this matter of placing the sexes upon an equality, so far as grounds for divorce are concerned. I wish to take the privilege of reading to the House one or two very short extracts. In the report of this commission I find this statement-
Apart from abstract justice the strongest reason for placing sexes on an equality is that, where two standards exist, there is a tendency to accept the lower for both parties. The social and economic position of women has greatly changed in the last hundred, and even in the last fifty years. The Married Women's Property Act, 1882, has given them a new status in regard to property; they engage freely in business and in the professions, and in municipal, educational and Poor Law administrations, and claim equality of treatment with men. In our opinion it is impossible to maintain a different standard of morality in the marriage relations, without creating the impression that justice is denied to women, an impression that must tend to lower the respect in which the marriage law is held by women.
488	COMMONS
Divorce
I suggest that the reasons given there apply with equal force to the conditions in Canada. I will read, in conclusion, the recommendation of that commission. It reads-
Our conclusion is that no satisfactory solution of the problem which is raised as to the personal relations between husband and wife can be found, except by placing them on an equal footing, and by declaring that, whatever grounds are permitted to a husband for obtaining a divorce from his wife, the same grounds shall be available to a wife in a suit against her husband. It may be safely left to a woman to consider whether she will exercise her rights, and it may reasonably be expected that, as has been proved by actual experience in Scotland, physical, social, pecuniary, and other considerations will have their natural effect, and lead to such rights not being exercised, at any rate in the great majority of cases, without such good and sufficient reason as will meet with the approval of relations and friends of the wife.
Now, actuated by the report of this commission, the English parliament in the year 1923 passed a law amending the Matrimonial Causes Act, and this clause was substituted for the provisions which I have previously referred to:
2. It shall be lawful for any wife to present a petition to the Court praying that her marriage may be dissolved on the ground that her husband has, since the celebration thereof and since the passing of this Act been guilty of adultery: Provided that nothing contained herein shall affect or take away any right of any wife, existing immediately before the passing of the Act.
That is all the legislation that this parliament needs to pass on the matter-simply that and nothing more. It will simply place the married woman in the four western provinces on a parity with the female applicants for divorce in the Maritime provinces and before this parliament of Canada. This is the only form in which redress can be given for that injustice. In my judgment justice calls imperatively that this parliament should take some action along the line indicated.

speechtext: I find myself in considerable agreement with the sentiments expressed by the speaker who introduced this resolution. He has reviewed the law as it exists in the various provinces of Canada, I think, fairly and reasonably. There exists in the Maritime provinces, as he has said, legislation inherited from the Old Land, that supplies that which he demands on behalf of woman in his resolution. The same exists to-day in the province of British Columbia. In section 5, chapter 67, there is a provision that a woman is entitled to judicial separation for an act of adultery on the part of her husband.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS

speechtext: My hon. friend is differentiating between judicial separation and absolute divorce. It is a different thing.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS

speechtext:
No, I did not attempt
to do that. I say she has the right to judicial separation in British Columbia. A large portion of my hon. friend's argument was devoted to the fact that woman found herself in a position where she was obliged to suffer humiliation, degradation and cruelty, that her life in fact was one of constant humiliation and misery; but there does exist, I think, in all the provinces of Canada-at least in the western provinces-a Married Woman's Protection Act, which provides that no woman is required to live with her husband when he is guilty of adultery. She can demand a separation from him and he must support and take care of her and her children; so that the only disadvantage a woman would be under in this case-and undoubtedly she is entitled to have that removed-would be the fact that she could not be married again. But, so far as that is concerned, she is not held down to a judicial separation. The Senate of Canada has always granted bills of divorce on a broader basis than that which was adopted in England. Adultery alone on the part of the husband has been always sufficient for the Senate committee of this parliament to grant a divorce.

In nearly all these cases where a woman makes application for divorce, there is, coupled with adultery, cruelty and desertion. Sinclair, in his book on Parliamentary Divorce in Canada at page 2, states:
Under the British North America Act, Canada obtained a constitution similar in principle to that of the United Kingdom, and within the limits of the subjects assigned to it the parliament of Canada is supreme, and its power is as plenary and ample as that of the parliament of the United Kingdom. While

in the exercise of such power the Canadian parliament has authority to grant divorces for any reason that may seem to it sufficient, still in exercising such authority, parliament is guided by and practically conforms to the principles upon which divorces are granted by the courts of England. This statement is, however, subject to this exception, that in Canada divorces are granted on the application of the wife on the sole ground of adultery, while in England, it is necessary that the adultery should be accompanied by cruelty or desertion, or the husband must have been guilty of incestuous adultery ...
And so on.

I believe, however, that as regards practical suffering of women under this act confined to such a small area in Canada and under the relief granted under our Senate divorce rules, there is actually very little suffering. As a general proposition laid down, I find myself pretty well in accord with the remarks of the hon. member who has moved the resolution, and my remarks on this occasion are simply to put the matter in such a way as to show what privileges a woman has at the present time in Canada by reason of the courts that exist., the laws existing in them and by reason of the Senate.

Mr. Speaker, I had no intention of saying anything in support of this resolution; but after listening to the remarks of the hon. member who has just taken his seat (Mr. McMurray) I felt compelled to say a few words. I listened very carefully to his remarks, and until he finished his last sentence I had no idea where he was going to land. He is in favour of the resolution, and I do not see why he cannot support it at the present time. It is a very simple resolution; it means simply to put a man and a woman on exactly the same footing. If I know anything about the laws of Canada, as regards the criminal laws, civil laws, or any other laws outside of the matter of divorce, I think a man and a woman are very much on the same footing. If a woman commits a crime, she is tried under the same laws and she suffers the same punishment. I cannot understand why in moral

Divorce
matters there should be any distinction between a man and a woman. I do not want to pose as a Puritan; but I think, simply as a matter of justice, this change should be no longer delayed. An hon. gentleman who spoke a little while ago said that this matter has been a long time in abeyance, so why bring it up at the present time? If it has been a long time in abeyance, the quicker it is brought up the better, and the quicker the matter is solved the better for everyone concerned. Often while reading some of these cases in the newspapers, I have felt myself burning with indignation at the injustice women were suffering in this respect, and I hope this matter can be successfully settled in the not far distant future as regards the four western provinces.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I did not intend to intervene in this debate, because in Nova Scotia we have a divorce court which we had and enjoyed prior to the advent of confederation. I do not believe any measure should be pursued which makes divorce easy. I need not refer to the scriptural admonition that says:
Whosoever shall put away his wife, saving for the cause of fornication, and shall marry another, com-mitteth adultery; and whosoever shall marry her that is divorced, committeth adultery.
It is very hard for a member to sit in the House of Commons and to find that his religious and also conscientious views regarding divorce are abused, because many of us are entirely opposed to the principle of divorce. I, therefore, believe that divorce should not be .made easy; but as regards the resolution of the hon. member for West Calgary (Mr. Shaw), I think it is absolutely fair. If we are going to have divorce in this country, if we must have it thrust upon us, there is no reason whatsoever why there should be a distinction between a man and a woman as regards the grounds for divorce. As I understand the argument of the hon. member for West Calgary, he says that the divorce courts in the West, came into existence a few years ago, and they find that to-day the women in the three western provinces are not on an equality with men as regards reasons for divorce. His object is that this parliament, which alone has control over marriage and divorce, shall bestow upon the courts of those provinces the right to give woman equality with man in regard to the reasons for securing divorce.
As I have already said, we in Nova Scotia have always had an equality in relation to men and women on this particular question.
I believe there are three grounds in the
fiVfr. Forke.]

province on which divorce may be secured. The law in Nova Scotia is based on the old English law and I believe that our people would resent any extension of it by providing further grounds for divorce. The three grounds I have mentioned are adultery, cruelty and impotence, or inability to consummate the marriage vow. Fortunately for us, the judge in divorce has always interpreted cruelty to mean adultery:	In other words, the
desire is to restrict as far as possible the grounds for granting divorce in that province. To me it is a matter of great delight to find that the court so inteiprets this particular law. What I think my hon. friend from West Calgary (Mr Scaw) is asking for is that the people of the provinces of Manitoba, Saskatchewan and Aiberta shall have the right to grant divorce to women on exactly the same grounds as divorce is granted to men. I have not followed the laws in those provinces and therefore I am unable to say what the law in this particular is in that section of the country. However, I am prepared to take my hon. friend's statement in this regard. Even if the hon. member is wrong in his interpretation of the law I feel that nothing is to be lest, by the parliament of Canada extending that power to those provinces. If we are go'ng to have divorces, then in the name of everything that is good, in the name of everything that is equitable, in the name of everything that is fair, let us confer upon the courts of the land the power to act in this matter so that those who want divorce may be able to go to those courts, where evidence can be properly adduced and these matters be decided upon, instead of having the parties come to Ottawa and the cases discussed in parliament. If we are to have divorces. I say, let the courts decide these questions Let us legislate on all other matters, but let us try as far as we can to keep the marrage vow inviolate.
Mr. S. W. JACOBS iGeorge Etienne Cartier) :	Coming as I Jo from the province
of Quebec, where divorce and rumours of divorce are very rarely heard, I could well afford to allow this resolution to pass without any remarks on my part. But inasmuch as this is a matter tnat concerns the parliament of Canada, a federal matter, I feel it is only right for me to rise in my place and declare that I am fully in agreement with the statements of the hon. member for West Calgary (Mr. Shaw) on the resolution he 5 p.m. has introduced to day. I could not help thinking, while the discussion

Divorce
was proceeding on this question, that if the parliament of Canada were only to adopt the old Levitical law there would be no question at all about the r'ghts of wife and husband. But I am afraid this will not be done, at least in my day and generation.
I have always beer in favour of perfect equality between the sexes both in regard to law and in all the relations of life. Now, why is it that we have a law declaring in favour of the man and against the woman, not only in this particular case but in many other respects? I will tell you: It is because the laws have been made by men. And I have no doubt that if women had made those laws they would have had a section similar to this declaring in favour of the woman against the man. Now that women have the right to sit in this House, I think we ought to recognize the advisability of making these changes as quickly as possible, before the ladies take the bit in their teeth, so to speak, when they get into the majority in this House, and make it very hard indeed for us. The law which my hon. frimd from West Calgary referred to, strange as it may seem, had its origin under the old Roman system. Under that system there was one law for men and another for women; there was one law for the Roman citizen and another for the stranger. This practice found its way into the civil law and the canon law m all European countries, and that explains why it was the law in England for hundreds of years. After the French Revolution the Code Napoleon changed the system; it is declared in the Code Napoleon, which is now the civil code of France, that women and men stand on an equal footing in the matter of divorce. Let me read to you the law of the province of Quebec. You will understand that there was never any revolution in the province of Quebec; that is to say, when the revolution in France took place Quebec had already become part and parcel cf the British Empire. Here is the law of the province of Quebec:
A husband may demand a separation on the ground of his wife's adulter!', and the wife may demand a separation on the ground of her husband's adultery, if he keeps his concubine in common habitation.
That is the law in Quebec to-day. In order that the wife should obtain a divorce from her husband she would have to show that the lady who lived under his protection was living in a domicile or home to which she the wife, had the right to repair if necessary. It is not necessary that he should bring the woman into the house where the wife lives; if it is shown that he has provided a habitation reserved especially for the lady upon
whom he confers his favours, then and only then has the wife the right to obtain a divorce. That would seem to be the law in the western provinces. My hon. friend the Minister of the Interior (Mr. Stewart, Argen-teuil) protests that it is not.

Why, let the stricken deer go weep,
The heart ungalled play;

I believe that both "must watch" and both "must sleep", but I am not in favour of one watching and the other sleeping; and for that reason I support the resolution, which I trust my hon. friend from West Calgary will introduce in the form of a bill. I am inclined to agree with the
Solicitor General (Mr. McMurray) in one particular; I think it is asking a great deal to ask the House to pass a resolution of this kind which must be in more or less indefinite form, as indeed the present resolution is. It would be much better if the hon. member for West Calgary (Mr. Shaw) would introduce a bill setting forth the changes which he desires to have made in the law. It seems to me that the Solicitor General and the hon. member for West Calgary almost got together on this question, but that there was a misunderstanding. I take it from what the mover of the resolution said that he desired an assurance from the Solicitor General that the bill which he would draft and which he was prepared to submit to the House would not be sidetracked, as so many bills have been, during previous sessions. He did not ask that the Solicitor General support the bill; he simply wanted the Solicitor General's assurance that the bill would be dealt with during the session, and I think that the Solicitor General might very well give that assurance.
Another statement was made by the hon. Solicitor General with which I am certainly not in accord. He said that the women of the western provinces have really no complaint because they could come to the Senate
Divorce

and get a divorce just as the men could and on the same grounds, without the necessity of proving desertion or cruelty. It is quite true-

speechtext: May I interrupt my hon. friend? I think he has misunderstood me. What I endeavoured to convey, whether I did it well or not, was that their situation was considerably modified by reason of the Married Women's Protection Act, and by reason of the fact that they could come to the Senate and secure a divorce. I did not say it was complete alleviation, but that it was a modification.

speechtext:
The Married Women's Protection Act has nothing to do with this matter. With regard to the married women of the western provinces having the right to come to Ottawa to secure a divorce, I may say that there have been a few cases where men and women have come from the West for that purpose. Last session a petition was presented by a woman who nominally resided at Vancouver, but who now I think, is temporarily in the Old Country. But these cases are very rare indeed, and the reason is obvious: the expense involved is prohibitive. People residing in British Columbia, for instance, can only in a few cases take advantage of the Senate procedure- that is, in cases where the petitioner has ample means. For my part I do not think that divorces should be granted by the Senate at all; it is not the proper way of handling the matter. All applications for divorces should be made to the courts, and there should be uniformity in regard to the granting of divorces. That suggestion has been discussed during previous sessions and there always seemed to be violent objection to it.
I presume that that objection was considered as well founded in the quarters from whence it came, but my point is that all matters of divorce should come before the courts; the petitioner should not be forced to come to Ottawa.
In regard to the arguments adduced by the hon. member for West Calgary (Mr. Shaw), they are unanswerable so far as they suggest that there should be the strictest equality as between man and woman and that the grounds of divorce should be the same in both instances.
ber for West Calgary should introduce this matter into the House in the form of a bill, and the member for West Calgary approved of the suggestion, provided that the Solicitor General would give an undertaking, not that the bill should pass, but that ample opportunity should be given for its consideration. To that the Solicitor General said that he would like to see the bill first. Well, whether the bill is a bad bill, a poor bill, or an ill-drafted bill, certainly it would be a bill touching an important matter which should merit the attention of the House, and I think the Solicitor General might well undertake that if the matter be brought before the House again in. the form of a bill, that bill will receive consideration this session. That would close the matter for the time being and allow us to proceed with other business.
In support of this suggestion let me just make these observations. I can well understand that there are men in this House who, through religious training or conscientious objection, believe that divorce should under no circumstances be granted. That is a perfectly reasonable position to take. It is not my own position, but that makes no difference; it is a position which may be assumed by reasonable persons who believe that it is better that some unhappily married people should "dree their weird'' rather than that divorce should be introduced. But, after all, we have divorce in this country; and that being the case it seems to me that we should have divorce on the most even basis of equality between husband and wife; that a man should be liable to be sued for divorce for precisely the same reasons as apply in the case of a woman.

The parliament of Canada grants divorces by special private acts. We grant them to men and women without distinction, men and women being subjected to precisely the same law. I understand that in Nova Scotia, where divorces are granted under provincial enactment, the law is equal between the sexes. In certain of the western provinces the law is not equal between the sexes, and that is the inequality and the injustice which the legislation shadowed forth in this resolution would cure. speechtext:
I cannot say that I disagree in any particular with the subject of the resolution before the House, nor can I say that I would be in favour of such a bill as the hon. member may see fit to introduce until I have had an opportunity of examining it. But it does seem to me strange' and rather an unusual condition of affairs when we examine the jurisdiction of the different provinces in this matter and the law that prevails to-day, and it seems to me that some remedy should be afforded, and that at once. We have in one province a certain law, interpreted in a certain way; in another province we have another law, interpreted in a different way; and in the province of Ontario we have no divorce law at all. Now, that seems to be an anomaly. We are all one people, living under the same general jurisdiction, and a man and a woman when they enter into the marriage contract undertake similar obligations, and I do not see why there should be any discrimination between the rights granted to a husband and those granted to a wife. It is an anomalous condition where we have one law in one province administered in a certain way, and another law in another province administered in a different way, and another province with no divorce law at all. That whole situation might very well be cleared up and one general law passed, saving, of course, those people in our Dominion who are entirely opposed to the granting of
divorces under any circumstances-one general law which would meet the whole situation, and under which the courts of the different provinces would have the same jurisdiction and the grounds upon which divorce could be granted should be clearly defined by Act of Parliament. Then, it seems to me, the rights of the two parties, the man and the woman, would be properly protected.

speechtext:
One of the greatest difficulties which the Fathers of Confederation had to contend with when the British North America Act was drafted was to overcome this question of divorce. Confederation was a union of provinces, and there was a strong opinion against divorce in both the old provinces of Ontario and Quebec, as there is to-day, not only among Roman Catholics but among Protestants as well. The spectacle we have witnessed here in the last few years, together with what is going on in the United States, should open the eyes of some of our thinking people. The Fathers of Confederation accepted divorce because it existed in Nova Scotia and New Brunswick, and a special clause was put into the act by which in certain cases the Dominion parliament could come to the relief of certain people without by that mere fact instituting divorce as a permanent institution in this land. Parliament took upon itself to come to the relief, and every divorce bill passed by this House has those words in its title-" An Act for the relief '' of such-and-such a party. In the years when I first attended parliament in this House it was customary when these bills were called- and they were far less numerous than they are to-day-for those who were opposed to divorce to enter their protest and call for a division at every step both in committee and in the whole House.
I know we are not discussing the merits of divorce, because a divorce law exists in certain of the provinces; but divorce was considered at that time a question of civil rights, and I question very much whether a law passed by this parliament would be operative in the province of Quebec, or whether divorce courts could be established in that province, because there would have to be a breach of the understanding of Confederation. However, what we are discussing now is merely a question of putting the woman on an equality with the man. Of course, I am opposed to divorce, always have been, and I am more opposed now than I ever was. In view of what is taking place in the United States and what seems to be
Divorce

taking place in Canada, but especially in the United States where one out of every ten or twelve marriages is dissolved-

I am not in favour of
divorce for a man or a woman. I am in favour of a system we have in the province of Quebec, which was described by the member for George Etienne Cartier (Mr. Jacobs) where if a man and woman cannot live together and they have certain valid reasons which are recognized by the courts, they can go before the courts and get a separation from bed and board. No divorce bill ever passes through this parliament without a second clause. Now what does that second clause say? It gives the right to marry again. That is the whole object. For these reasons I do not think it would be fair to ask this House to accept this resolution, and especially

to ask the Solicitor General to bind himself to support any bill that is not before the House.

I did not intend to speak on this
question because I feel it is an injustice against woman brought about by man, and I want the men unassisted by what I say to remove that injustice as I am sure they will do. The member for George Etienne Cartier told the exact truth when he said that the cause of this was that the law had beeD made by men- When you read the laws, nol only this but a great many others, and read history, you will find they are everywhere the handiwork of men, describing their own actions and forgetting that after all they are only half of the great human family.

I would not say that. The hon. member who sits across the way (Mr. Marcil) is anxious that divorces should be made fewer instead of more. I had written on a piece of paper here just the question that the hon. member for East Calgary (Mr. Irvine) asked my hon. friend when he was speaking, that is, would he be willing to put men on the same basis in the four western provinces as women are in regard to divorce? If he is willing to do that it will remove restrictions and result in bringing about equality between the sexes. The very fact that men would take this step to place women on an equal footing with themselves will in itself have the effect of bringing about a feeling of good will. I think men hardly realize how deep in the heart of women is buried the resentment which they all feel against what they know to be an injustice, not only in this particular matter but in other things. That is one of the causes for the great woman's movement throughout the world. Women have felt that only by organizing and influencing public sentiment in this way could they obtain justice for themselves.
I therefore ask hon. members to adopt this resolution out of a sense of justice for women and a proper regard for the spirit of fair play.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS
subsubtopic: EQUALITY OF GROUNDS FOR RELIEF AS BETWEEN THE SEXES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am entirely opposed
to the resolution of the hon. member for West Calgary (Mr. Shaw). I think it is liable to have a pernicious influence because its object is to give freer access to divorce.
It is quite evident that by this resolution, we are subject to increase the number of divorces in certain provinces of the Dominion. Con-

Divorce
sequently, by creating opportunities for divorce cases to be submitted to the courts, we countenance, after all, the theory of divorce. This is why I am opposed to this resolution.
Divorce is certainly contrary to the divine laws and the laws of man. It has proved a great calamity to those countries that have adopted such a means. It is unfortunately the scourge of modern times. It assails at its very root home life which is the foundation of society itself. It is quite easy to perceive to what a disastrous end would lead such legislation opening a wider door to divorce. Canada is a Christian country and the countenancing of divorce would tend to the destruction of the conjugal ties which is a fundamental part of Christianity.
So far as the province of Quebec is concerned, our laws are entirely opposed to divorce. It is true, as it was mentioned by one of the hon. members who spoke before me, that the Civil Code of Quebec recognizes separation on well defined grounds; but the tendency of courts is to restrict as much as possible this recourse and section 185 of the Civil Code lays down the following rule.
Marriage can only be dissolved by the natural death of one of the parties; while both live, it is indissoluble.
A previous speaker recalled rightly, the principles which guided the Fathers of Confederation in matters of divorce. In a conciliatory mood, the British North America Act included a measure to allow divorce in certain cases, but the Fathers of Confederation had not in mind the introduction of this measure so as to favour and pave the way for divorce, neither was this measure introduced with the aim of spreading the demand for divorce. The adoption of this resolution, under the plea of placing the two sexes on the same footing, would tend to generalize the pernicious principle of divorce in our country.
There is no need of recalling the history of the different measures which have been moved in this House since confederation aiming at enlarging on the Act authorizing divorce, under the British North America Act. On all occasions, when this House was requested, for instance, to establish a special divorce court in certain provinces all our statesmen opposed it. Sir John A. Macdonald, himself, in 1875 and later on, rose in this House to declare that there should be no legislation of a nature to facilitate divorce and make it a more common practice in any shape or form. I think we are faithful to those guiding principleswhich have always been proclaimed by all statesmen throughout the country-in opposing the resolution of the hon. member for West Calgary.
Whatever movement is undertaken in this country to encourage divorce, it becomes an outrage to the conscience of 2,500,000 Catholics. This minority is required to live in the midst of the majority and it has a right to the respect of its religious convictions. I therefore, strongly oppose this resolution and I still hope that the hon. member for West Calgary will be persuaded to withdraw this resolution; I am convinced that if we are called upon to vote this resolution will certainly be defeated.
Mr. PIERRE F. CASGRAIN (Charlevoix and Montmorency) (Translation):	Mr. Speaker before this resolution carries, I think it is the duty of the representatives of Quebec to express the views of that province on this question. We have already heard from the hon. member for George Etienne Cartier (Mr. Jacobs), the hon. member for Bonaventure (Mr. Marcil), the hon. member for Brome (Mr. McMaster), and the hon. member for Labelle (Mr. Fortier). They have respectively expressed their opinion on the subject. The hon. member for Bonaventure (Mr. Marcil) rightly stated that this question is of paramount importance, and dates back to confederation.
He pointed out that, when it was a question of the union of the Canadian provinces, this problem was fully debated and was closely studied by the most eminent men, Sir John A. Macdonald, Sir George Etienne Cartier and all the Fathers of Confederation. If this question was so important on such a memorable occasion as to when it was a matter of the union of all the provinces, to have been a cause of discussion, and even of dissension-which finally disappeared following protracted conferences and a long delay-I think we should not be too hasty in adopting, to-day, the resolution which is before the House. Those who suggested to the hon. member for West Calgary (Mr. Shaw) the introduction of a bill with reference to this question, so that a discussion might take place in a proper way on such an important matter, are quite right.
In the province of Quebec the separation may be granted for certain specific and defined reasons. We have no divorce court. Some years ago, when we were in the opposition, I remember that the ex-member for Kingston, to-day the Attorney General for the province of Ontario, introduced a bill aiming at the establishment of divorce courts
Divorce

in mis country. I recall that all the hon. members of the province of Quebec, even those who do not share our religious convictions, voted against this bill; not that this measure was against their religious beliefs, but because it carried with it a tendency to increase divorce cases, in such a way as to undermine the fundamental basis of society.
The hon. member for George Etienne Cartier (Mr. Jacobs) has pointed out the specific reasons which enable a person to obtain a separation in the province of Quebec. That province has always kept up the French laws and the Code Napoleon, and I am not aware that we have ever found fault against the law as it exists. The hon. member for La-belle (Mr. Fortier), who has just preceded me in this debate, referred to the section of the Civil Code which declares that marriage may only be dissolved by death. We have often heard it said, on many an occasion: When a person marries, it is "For better or for worse."

Will tell

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS
subsubtopic: EQUALITY OF GROUNDS FOR RELIEF AS BETWEEN THE SEXES
speechtext:
It is for life; it is exactly what I say. Indeed, one of the sections of our Civil Code specifies that marriage can only be dissolved by death. The axiom that I have just quoted and to which my hon. friend drew my attention, is a way of expressing oneself. When marriage has been consecrated, if the union is happy or unhappy, the contracting parties must accept the accomplished fact. In a number of cases, notwithstanding that there might have been reasons for which persons might have asked for divorce, they have been well advised to have recourse to separation. As the hon. member for Bonaventure (Mr. Marcil) expressed it this afternoon: often parsons who seek divorce have in mind and desire to remarry.
The hon. member for Southeast Grey (Miss Macphail) spoke just now on this subject to vindicate the rights of women and claim justice, equal rights for all. I sincerely congratulate her on the way she unfolded her arguments in the name of all those whom she has the honour to represent, and whose interpreter she is for the whole Dominion, being the only representative of her sex in the Canadian parliament. I congratulate her,

I say, for the way she gave the reasons which militate in favour of womanhood, in the western provinces, so that they may be placed on the same footing as man. I congratulate her, but I cannot entirely side with her, because notwithstanding all legislation or law which might be adopted, aiming to grant women the same rights as men, there will always remain a difference, something which will not be identical. This difference exists since the creation of man. There has always existed and there will always exist in woman, an inborn weakness, a marked inferiority. I am not saying this with the idea of depreciating woman, because we have all had mothers. And we know that if woman, notwithstanding her nature and weakness, may render services to her country, we are also aware that she is unable to accomplish as much as men. On the other hand, woman, is looked upon-and with reason-as the angel of the home, as a gentler being than man.

Physiologically
