maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS
subsubtopic: EQUALITY OF GROUNDS FOR RELIEF AS BETWEEN THE SEXES
speechtext:
Yes,
physiologically, to use the right expression of the hon. member for Lotbiniere (Mr. Vien). In spite of our granting the franchise to woman, in spite of our placing her on the same footing as man, in all spheres of action, notwithstanding that we grant her the same rights and the same privileges, it is not less certain that you will never be able to pass a law making woman equal to man. The latter will always have that superiority which characterizes him and places him at the head of society. And even in the home, although woman is the queen, although she is the one who brings up the children, although she is the one who, very often, through her advice, prevents her husband from blundering, is it not, finally, man that is the master?
The hon. member, Sir, for Drummond and Arthabaska (Mr. Laflamme) has, at the out-

Divorce
set of this debate, twice, put a question, to the hon. member for Brome (Mr. McMaster), and he insisted on the fact that if the resolution of the hon. member for West Calgary (Mr. Shaw) was adopted, and, if a bill based on this resolution was introduced, what would happen in the western provinces, would be that divorce could be obtained still more easily. The hon. member for Drummond and Arthabaska (Mr. Laflamme), with whom I am well acquainted, a man who has a wide knowledge of men, women and the world, one of the greatest criminal lawyers in this country, who understands the human heart and human nature, fears that if we open any wider the door to allow certain persons to dissolve the ties of marriage, it might, perhaps, be to their detriment and to that of society. I am of the same opinion as the hon. member for Drummond and Arthabaska. As I stated at the outset of my remarks, the principle of the present resolution is the same as the one which was at stake in 1919 or 1920, at the time of the debate introduced by Mr. Nickle, then member for Kingston.
If I am not mistaken the hon. member for West Calgary, in introducing this resolution, wishes to obtain relief for certain wrongs which exist in the western provinces. I do not think that he will succeed, not that the religion of the majority of those who sit on your right, Sir, are opposed to divorce; but because I notice that many of the members belonging to a different religion than ours, share in a way our views on this question. I, therefore, ask the House to postpone the continuation of this debate to a future date, so that we may consider the subject in all its phases and from all angles. We cannot and must not, on such an important question, express an opinion lightly, as we are asked to do, for the excellent reason that it might, perhaps, sanction a principle and acknowledge a fact which, next year, might serve as a precedent to ask this House the adoption of another bill or another resolution to still widen the door and give more facility to all who, for very vague reasons wish to obtain a divorce. It gives me much pleasure to proclaim in this House and throughout the country that I firmly believe in the teachings of the religion to which I have the honour to belong, and as for myself as well as for the majority of the members who sit on your right, Sir, I believe that if we were ever asked to vote on a similar measure as the one now before us, we could not act otherwise than the way we did 32
in the past, when a similar measure was introduced in the House, that is to vote against any measure which might appear to be a sanction of the principle of divorce. Again do I state our beliefs would not allow us to do otherwise. It is impossible for us to force our conscience to accept a measure which, looking at it from all angles, would injure the principles of our religion, principles that we have sworn to safeguard when we were baptised and confirmed.
It was stated in the course of this debate, that it would be preferable to have a uniform legislation and create special divorce courts throughout the country, as they exist all over, where the people of the various provinces might register their complaints. It is a repetition of the same thing. These bills or resolutions only aim at opening the door to divorce, making it easier and less costly to obtain. There is a desire to increase the causes of disunion and quarrels which exist in our country instead of decreasing them. I think they exist enough, to-day, without trying to increase them by adopting such a resolution without making a deeper study of the question. I have, perhaps, been repeating the arguments already brought out by speakers who have preceded me in this debate, however, I think, Sir, that we should not adopt the resolution of the hon. member for West Calgary, under the present circumstances, when it is introduced at the beginning of the session, and a great number of members have hardly had time to digest the debate on the Address, and have not had time to carefully consider this question as it should be. I have, perhaps, expressed on this subject views which may seem contrary to those of the hon. members who sit on your left, Sir, but it is permissible to differ in opinion from our colleagues. By virtue of the British principles which govern us, and which have united the Dominion, everybody is free to think and to freely express his thoughts. That is what we wish to do. There lies the reason that I was not backward, a moment ago in stating that any measure or resolution the object of which is to weaken the ties of marriage and to do away with the impediments to divorce, would be legislation of a pernicious character. It is preferable that a few should suffer, rather than spread a plague existing in a number of countries and which threatens to attack us, if we do not strive to restrain and check it. What is happening in the great American republic? The ease with which divorce is granted in the case of many persons having married thoughtlessly.

Divorce

A great number of soldiers were married in this way in Europe, during the war; immediately after their return to this country, they perceived their error and took the means of obtaining a divorce. And we now witness a great number of broken homes, families separated and persons who will lead a miserable existence for the remainder of their lives, who will make their wives and progeny unhappy and be a desgrace and dishonour to their families.
I would have liked, Sir, to be better prepared to carry on this discussion and I must beg your indulgence and that of the members of this House, and if I have not given to this question the preparation which so important a subject deserves, it is that I did not think that this resolution would be brought up to-day and that we would be called upon to express our views immediately on such a serious subject. This is the reason, Sir, that I have not before me the statistics that I wished to quote and that I have neither, perhaps, brought out the most convincing reasons, the best and strongest arguments for the solving of a problem having such import.
We heard, as I mentioned, a moment ago, a number' of the oldest members of this House-among others the hon. member for Bonaventure-who gave their reasons, in the name of their fellow citizens and constituencies which they represent, why they oppose such a measure. For the same reasons, in the name of my fellow citizens of the province of Quebec and the electors of the county which I represent, I, myself, must disapprove of this resolution. Its principle seems to me wrong. I do not think a vote will be taken on it, to-day, and, therefore, when the debate will again come up, I shall be better prepared and shall give stronger reasons to have it rejected. I even question, if the hon. member for West Calgary, wishing to do justice to the citizens of the provinces which he mentioned in his speech, is not rather doing them irreparable injury in the near future? I am fully convinced, Sir, that the resolution of the hon. member will not in any possible way better the situation which he has described.
As it is six o'clock, Sir, I move the adjournment of the debate.
Motion agreed to and debate ajoumed.
At six o'clock the House adjourned, without question being put, pursuant to rule.
